newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - US retail sales seen tapering off in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - US retail sales seen tapering off in '97.

text.p: U.S. retailers might see slightly slower sales growth in 1997 even though consumers should remain decidedly upbeat, experts said.
While shoppers are expected to flock to stores this holiday season, demand will likely taper off in the new year.

"I sense that (retailers) are going to end up the year quite well and will be overly optimistic for 1997," said Howard Eilenberg, retail analyst at LJR Redbook Research. He predicted retailers will beef up first-quarter inventories, get stuck with merchandise and end up cutting prices.

William Griggs, managing director of Griggs & Santow Inc, said he expects less strength in the sale of durables as automobile purchases will not be quite as strong after two consecutive years of relatively good demand.
However, he added, "I think consumers will be still picking up the non-durables."
Consumers, encouraged by low unemployment, modest price pressures and continued wage growth, have sported a bullish outlook that some experts predict will largely carry over into 1997.
As of October, 1996, total retail sales had increased 5.2 percent from last year's leve, according to the latest Commerce Department figures.
A Reuters survey of 10 analysts produced an average forecast calling for total sales to rise 4.5 percent in 1997.
This forecast partly reflects consumer behavior during the advanced stage of the business cycle.
"We're in the mature phase of an expansion," said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.
Without pent-up demand as a catalyst, spending will likely track income growth, she said.

The lastest Conference Board report said consumers are more positive about current business conditions than at any time in this decade. Its U.S. consumer confidence index held steady at 107.3 in November, unchanged from October.
"There's nothing signaling a sudden change any time soon," said Lynn Franco, associate director of the Conference Board's Consumer Research Center.

"We may see somewhat of a drop but it's going to be more due to a shifting within the components rather than a signal that the economy is getting worse or consumers are growing increasingly tentative," she added.
Franco explained that the present situation component, at a seven-year high in November, may decline, and unless the expectations component picks up the slack, the overall index will fall.
Last month, the Commerce Department reported the economy expanded at a 2.0 percent annualized pace in the third quarter after growing by 4.7 percent in the second quarter.

Norwest Corp chief economist Sung Won Sohn said he expects slower growth in 1997. "Modest economic growth (and) higher interest rates will probably make for somewhat lower consumer confidence and then slower growth in retail sales."

Griggs agrees economic growth will probably slow next year, but he also predicted fewer high-profile layoffs, continued low unemployment and perhaps bipartisian cooperation on tackling the budget deficit.
"I think it all becomes a part of what looks like a fairly attractive environment...," he said. "So, I don't see any reason to think the mood doesn't stay pretty good."
